what it is: Surfaces and their buffers. The base object every client needs.
how om_wm handles it: CompositorState. Commits are queued in State::committed and drained once per frame by the render side.

what it is: Shared memory buffers: pixels through a file descriptor. The universal fallback path.
how om_wm handles it: ShmState. take_shm_buffer copies into a texture we own, so the client's buffer is released immediately.

what it is: Input devices as a group: pointer, keyboard, touch.
how om_wm handles it: SeatState with a pointer and a keyboard. No touch: this machine has none, and a canvas would want its own answer for it.

what it is: The screen: size, scale, refresh. Toolkits refuse to map a window without one.
how om_wm handles it: One output the size of the screen, scale 1, even though the canvas is unbounded. It is what clients size themselves against.

what it is: Clipboard and drag and drop.
how om_wm handles it: DataDeviceState. Focus is handed to it on every focus change or the clipboard points at the wrong window. No primary selection on purpose: its only use is middle-click paste, and middle click belongs to the canvas.

what it is: Application windows: xdg_toplevel, xdg_popup, and the configure handshake.
how om_wm handles it: XdgShellState. Toplevels become quads on the canvas; popups and subsurfaces are children placed off their parent every frame. Move, resize and maximize requests are queued and answered by the canvas code.

what it is: GPU buffers passed as file descriptors, with no copy.
how om_wm handles it: DmabufState with a v4 feedback global, which Mesa requires. Imported as EGLImages and sampled in place, or copied into a texture we own while minified so it can carry a mip chain.

what it is: A client cropping or scaling its own surface.
how om_wm handles it: ViewporterState. Registered because toolkits expect it; nothing in the canvas code reads it yet, which is a gap if a client ever uses it in anger.

what it is: One application asking that another's window be focused, with a token proving a user asked.
how om_wm handles it: XdgActivationState. Tokens older than 30s are refused. An activated window takes focus, and the view flies to it when it is not already fully on screen.

what it is: Pinch and swipe as sequences a client can follow, rather than as scroll it has to guess at.
how om_wm handles it: PointerGesturesState. A pinch the canvas is not using is forwarded to the window under the pointer as a real begin/update/end sequence.

what it is: A client naming a cursor ("text", "grab") instead of sending pixels.
how om_wm handles it: CursorShapeManagerState. The name is looked up in the same Xcursor theme the canvas pointer comes from, once per shape, hits and misses both remembered.

what it is: Surfaces belonging to the screen rather than to the window stack: bars, launchers, notification daemons. Anchors, layers and exclusive zones.
how om_wm handles it: Nothing. Quickshell, waybar, fuzzel and mako all refuse to start without it. Smithay has the protocol side and a layer map that does the arranging, so the work is a handler plus deciding what the four layers mean on an infinite canvas. This is the natural home for anything pinned to the view.

what it is: A lock screen the compositor trusts: the locker owns the screen and a crash leaves it locked.
how om_wm handles it: Nothing. Smithay has session_lock. Needed before this is a machine anyone else uses.

what it is: Screenshots and screen recording by another program.
how om_wm handles it: Nothing. om_wm can grab its own framebuffer with Super+S, which is not the same thing: no other application can capture.

what it is: Negotiating who draws the titlebar, client or server.
how om_wm handles it: Nothing, so every client draws its own. That is why we draw the shadow they pad around themselves. Worth having if the canvas ever wants uniform chrome.

what it is: Fractional output scaling, negotiated rather than rounded.
how om_wm handles it: Nothing. We advertise scale 1 and the canvas zoom does the scaling instead, which is a different model and mostly a better one here.

what it is: Telling a client exactly when its frame reached the screen.
how om_wm handles it: Nothing. Clients that pace themselves on it fall back to frame callbacks, which we do send.

what it is: Raw pointer motion with no cursor position: the other half of pointer lock.
how om_wm handles it: Nothing. Smithay has it.

what it is: Locking or confining the pointer to a surface. Games, 3D viewports, drag handles.
how om_wm handles it: Nothing. Listed in TODO.txt as "correct pointer lock behaviour" and needs relative_pointer alongside it.

what it is: Input methods: any language that is not typed one key to one letter.
how om_wm handles it: Nothing. A blocker for anyone typing CJK, and not optional for a distro.

what it is: Letting a panel see and control other windows: task lists, window switchers.
how om_wm handles it: Nothing. Would be needed by any bar we ship once layer shell exists.

what it is: A client asking the screen not to blank, and telling one how long the user has been idle.
how om_wm handles it: Nothing, and nothing blanks the screen yet either, so neither is felt.

what it is: A one pixel buffer of a solid colour, so a client can fill an area without allocating.
how om_wm handles it: Nothing, despite the module header claiming otherwise. Cheap to add and used by some toolkits for backgrounds.

what it is: A client saying its surface is video or a game, so the compositor can adapt.
how om_wm handles it: Nothing. Interesting later for deciding what to do about tearing and vsync.

what it is: A client asking to present without waiting for vblank.
how om_wm handles it: Nothing. Related to the multimonitor and flip work parked in TODO.txt.

what it is: A client labelling a window so the compositor can apply rules to it across restarts.
how om_wm handles it: Nothing. The closest thing to a window declaring what kind of thing it is, which is what picture in picture actually needs instead of matching titles.

what it is: Marking a window as a modal dialog, and giving a window an icon.
how om_wm handles it: Nothing. Both small, both nice once there is any chrome or window list to show them in.

what it is: One client referring to another's window, so a dialog can be parented across processes.
how om_wm handles it: Nothing. Portals use it.

what it is: Tagging a client as sandboxed, so the compositor can treat it with less trust.
how om_wm handles it: Nothing. Matters the day a distro ships flatpaks.

what it is: Handing a whole output to a client, for headsets.
how om_wm handles it: Nothing, and probably never.

what it is: X11 applications, through an X server the compositor drives.
how om_wm handles it: Nothing at all: no xwayland_shell, no X server. Any X-only application simply cannot run here.
